title: An Annealing-based Quantum Neural Network with Discrete Wavelet Transforms for Enhanced Air Pollution Nowcasting
authors: Otto Menegasso Pires, André Saimon, Daniela Herrmann, Prashant Kumar, Marcelo Moret, Erick Giovani Sperandio Nascimento
abstract: Air pollution poses a significant threat to public health, exacerbated by the rapid industrialization and urbanization of modern society. While traditional deep learning offers predictive capabilities, recent advancements in quantum machine learning (QML) present a compelling alternative. Here, we introduce a scalable hybrid framework that integrates variational quantum circuits with quantum annealing. Leveraging a neuromorphic quantum computing platform to transcend the qubit limitations of the NISQ era, we model particulate matter (PM$_{2.5}$) dynamics using high-density urban data from the UK. We demonstrate that our Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) exhibit an intrinsic resilience to input volatility, significantly outperforming classical baselines (MLP and LSTM) on raw, high-entropy environmental data. Furthermore, we successfully scaled the model to 172 qubits, observing a synergistic enhancement when coupled with wavelet decomposition that achieves state-of-the-art predictive fidelity. These findings establish a critical benchmark for quantum utility, proving that scalable, neuromorphic quantum machine learning can now address complex, non-linear real-world problems.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid annealing-based quantum neural network, especially when combined with discrete wavelet transforms, can improve PM2.5 air-pollution nowcasting on noisy urban data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests a scalable quantum machine-learning route for real-world environmental forecasting where classical models struggle with high-entropy, volatile inputs.
method: Variational quantum circuits integrated with quantum annealing on a neuromorphic quantum computing platform
PM2.5 nowcasting using high-density urban data from the UK
Discrete wavelet decomposition to enhance predictive performance and scale to 172 qubits
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the QNN outperformed MLP and LSTM baselines on raw environmental data and achieved state-of-the-art fidelity when combined with wavelet decomposition at 172 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Performance claims should be interpreted with care because scaling and reproducibility on other datasets, hardware platforms, and longer forecasting horizons may be challenging.
infographic.paper_title: An Annealing-based Quantum Neural Network with Discrete Wavelet Transforms for Enhanced Air Pollution Nowcasting

title: Benchmarking Modular Optimization Strategies for Parameterized Quantum Circuits
authors: Carla Cotea, Stefan Balauca, Andreea Arusoaie
abstract: Training parameterized quantum circuits requires balancing optimization progress with limited evaluation budgets and the statistical uncertainty of near-term quantum hardware. We present a modular benchmarking framework that separates quantum search-direction estimation from classical parameter-update rules, allowing their interactions and sensitivities to be examined independently. We evaluate a suite of gradient-based, stochastic, and derivative-free optimizers across combinatorial optimization using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), supervised quantum machine learning using Iris classification and a quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) for binary MNIST classification, and quantum chemistry using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for molecular hydrogen. By separating objective evaluations from sample-circuit costs under finite-shot simulation and physical execution on a 156-qubit processor, we compare optimizer behavior across workloads with different parameter counts and measurement requirements. Four selected simulator and hardware case studies report terminal and best observed objectives separately, alongside post-training classifier accuracies. The comparisons include selected MaxCut and hydrogen trajectories and illustrate workload-dependent objective changes and evaluation costs, while the simulator benchmark compares both peak and mean performance across three seeds. The hardware runs do not establish an optimizer ranking or isolate a causal effect of device noise.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that optimizer performance for parameterized quantum circuits depends strongly on separating quantum search-direction estimation from classical parameter-update rules, so the best method is workload- and budget-dependent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This modular benchmarking framework helps engineers compare optimizers fairly across QAOA, QML, QCNN, and VQE under finite-shot and hardware constraints.
method: Benchmarked gradient-based, stochastic, and derivative-free optimizers
Decoupled direction-estimation from update rules to study interactions independently
Compared simulation and 156-qubit hardware runs across MaxCut, Iris, MNIST, and H2
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports terminal and best-observed objectives, classifier accuracies, and selected trajectory plots, with simulator results aggregated over three seeds and hardware evaluated by objective and cost under finite-shot execution.
infographic.watch_item: The hardware experiments should not be read as an optimizer ranking, since the abstract explicitly notes they do not isolate causal effects of device noise.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Modular Optimization Strategies for Parameterized Quantum Circuits

title: Verifiable Sampling for Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Matteo Inajetovic, Anna Pappa, Petros Wallden
abstract: Generative machine learning has shown remarkable results across a wide range of interdisciplinary tasks, motivating significant efforts toward Quantum Generative Models as a path to beyond-classical performance, given their capability of generating classically intractable distributions. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to securely delegating such computations to a powerful remote quantum server. In this work, we propose a blind and verifiable protocol for sampling that can be used for the inference phase of such quantum models. Such a protocol inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and achieves verifiability by exploiting known approaches based on trapification schemes. Alongside, to delegate the training phase, we discuss an extension of the previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026). Beyond the usual Accept/Abort outcome characterizing verification protocols, the sampling protocol for inference also provides, even against a malicious server, an estimation of the amount of corrupted generated samples, i.e., a fine-grained feature describing the quality of the outcome connecting verification protocols and application-level benchmarking.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a blind, verifiable protocol for delegating generative quantum model sampling, enabling secure inference on an untrusted quantum server.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical security layer for quantum generative workflows by combining privacy, verifiability, and a finer-grained estimate of sample corruption.
method: Use Universal Blind Quantum Computing to hide the client’s computation from the server.
Add trapification-based verifiability to detect malicious deviations during sampling.
Extend prior verifiable delegated variational quantum algorithms to cover training-phase delegation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a protocol with an Accept/Abort verification outcome and an additional estimate of the fraction of corrupted generated samples under malicious behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is protocol-level and may require substantial quantum resources and careful trap/infrastructure design to be practical on near-term hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Verifiable Sampling for Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning

title: Dynamical Lie Algebras for Fixed-Gate Quantum Ansätze
authors: Orlane Zang, Daniel Juteau, Tony Quertier, Grégoire Barrué
abstract: Parameterized Quantum Circuits have emerged as a central framework for variational quantum algorithms in the NISQ regime, with major applications in quantum simulation, combinatorial optimization, and, more recently, quantum machine learning (QML). By developing a new approach for computing dynamical Lie algebras associated with quantum circuits combining parametrized gates and non-parametrized entangling gates, we aim to extend the applicability of recent algebraic results to architectures that are actually used in quantum machine learning.

infographic.key_insight: The paper extends dynamical Lie algebra analysis to hybrid quantum ansätze that mix parametrized and fixed entangling gates, matching architectures used in quantum machine learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical algebraic tool for assessing expressivity and controllability of NISQ-era circuits before deployment in variational and QML workflows.
method: Develop a new method to compute dynamical Lie algebras for circuits with both parametrized and non-parametrized gates.
Target fixed-gate entangling architectures commonly used in quantum machine learning.
Extend recent Lie-algebraic results beyond purely parametrized circuit families.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract positions the contribution as a method extension rather than reporting experimental benchmarks, so validation appears to be theoretical and architecture-focused.
infographic.watch_item: The approach may be harder to scale or apply efficiently on large circuits if Lie-algebra computation becomes combinatorially expensive.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamical Lie Algebras for Fixed-Gate Quantum Ansätze

title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Quantum Neural Network Configurations for Financial Time Series Forecasting
authors: Jack Waller, Xing Liang, Dimitrios Makris, Rajagopal Nilavalan
abstract: Quantum machine learning, and quantum neural networks (QNNs) in particular, are advancing fields with growing potential. Although systematic comparisons of QNN configurations have been explored primarily for classification tasks, comparatively little attention has been given to regression problems, particularly financial time series forecasting. This study presents a large-scale systematic comparative evaluation of QNN component configurations for financial time series forecasting, using the GBP/USD spot exchange rate as a case study. A grid search across encoding methods, ansatz designs, qubit counts, layer depths, and cost functions yields 1,368 distinct model configurations, each evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational cost, and convergence behaviour. The results reveal unique insights into how the choice of methods influences performance, such as that gate selection and arrangement are more critical to model success than raw parameter count, and that entanglement is a system-level property of the full circuit rather than solely at the ansatz level. The best-performing QNN configuration achieves an $R^2$ score of 0.985, outperforming a classical BiLSTM baseline. Additionally, the impact of real quantum hardware noise is assessed through execution on the IQM Emerald device, revealing that gate errors and decoherence represent a significant barrier to practical deployment, with gate selection and circuit depth identified as key determinants of hardware noise resilience. Overall, the findings provide practical architectural guidance for QNN design and establish a baseline characterisation of QNN noise sensitivity on near-term quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: For financial time series forecasting, QNN performance depends more on circuit design choices—especially gate type, arrangement, and entanglement structure—than on simply increasing parameter count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study gives practical design guidance for building more accurate and hardware-resilient QNNs, while also showing where near-term quantum devices still face noise-related deployment limits.
method: Grid-searched 1,368 QNN configurations across encodings, ansatzes, qubit counts, depths, and cost functions.
Evaluated each model on GBP/USD forecasting using prediction accuracy, computational cost, and convergence behaviour.
Tested selected configurations on real quantum hardware (IQM Emerald) to assess noise sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark reports a best QNN achieving R² = 0.985, outperforming a classical BiLSTM baseline, while also characterizing hardware noise effects on real-device runs.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising but practical deployment remains constrained by gate errors, decoherence, and sensitivity to circuit depth on current quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Quantum Neural Network Configurations for Financial Time Series Forecasting

title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Hoong Chuin Lau
abstract: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are limited by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and the difficulty of encoding constraints, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. We call such workflows adaptive: decisions conventionally fixed in advance, from formulation and penalties to shot budgets, backends, and whether to invoke a quantum processor at all, are made by learned policies that respond to the instance, the progress of the solve, or the hardware. This review examines three paradigms, AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization, and organizes the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application. A structured search identified a 119-paper corpus, of which 67 papers form an evidence core coded in detail. The evidence is considerably stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for the reverse direction: learning already reduces quantum evaluations, improves initialization, supports decomposition and penalty control, and mitigates noise, whereas evidence that quantum computation improves learned optimizers remains largely confined to small-scale simulation. Experimental controls are thin: of 52 studies in the three paradigms, 22 include no classical baseline, the quantum contribution is fully isolated in 10 of 24 where an ablation applies, and the median largest experiment uses 16 qubits. We introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy, from simulation to practical quantum advantage, and find no broadly convincing result at the highest level. We argue that scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive, learned control of quantum optimization workflows is more promising today than using quantum computers to directly improve learning-based optimizers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For combinatorial optimization systems, the main design problem is now allocating classical and quantum resources dynamically across formulation, sampling, backend selection, and stopping decisions.
method: Structured review of 119 papers, with 67 coded in an evidence core
Organized literature by the decision being learned: formulation, penalties, shot budgets, backend choice, and quantum invocation
Introduced an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy to rank results from simulation to practical quantum advantage
infographic.evidence_signal: Evidence is stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for quantum-for-AI; among 52 studies, 22 had no classical baseline, only 10 of 24 ablations isolated the quantum contribution, and the median largest experiment used 16 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Results remain limited by small-scale experiments, thin baselines, and weak isolation of quantum effects, so claims of real-world advantage should be treated cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization

title: Decoder- and Noise-Aware Optimization Framework for Clifford-Deformed Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Julius Rye Bønnelykke, Benjamin Joecker, Peter Krogstrup, Vincent Philippe Michal, Mark Kamper Svendsen
abstract: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computing requires qubit-efficient quantum error correction (QEC). Clifford deformations (CDs) modify the stabilizers of a QEC code to lower its logical error rate at no additional resource cost. However, the number of possible CDs grows exponentially with the number of qubits, making exhaustive search infeasible beyond small codes. In this work, we further show that under circuit level noise the optimal CD depends strongly on both the noise model and decoder. To make systematic CD optimization possible, we introduce Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient search algorithm that treats the circuit, noise model and decoder as a black box. We benchmark EBBI's performance on the rotated surface code, under two strongly $Z$-biased circuit-level noise models with the PyMatching decoder. At distance 3, EBBI finds the optimal CD using up to $\sim 1100\times$ fewer shots than random search. At distance 5, when run at the target error rate, the median EBBI run converges to the CDs we believe to be optimal, while random search never converges. Under a $Z$-biased SI1000-like noise model, EBBI discovers a new CD, the B-XZZX code, which we generalized to larger distances. It differs from XZZX on only a fraction $\mathcal{O}(d^{-1})$ of the qubits at code distance $d$, yet its relative advantage grows from $\approx 5\%$ at $d = 3$ to $\approx 12\%$ at $d = 11$. We thus show that the B-XZZX pattern found by EBBI can be systematically scaled to larger code distances. Our work represents a first step towards scalable CD optimization for general QEC codes.

infographic.key_insight: A decoder- and noise-aware search can efficiently find Clifford deformations that substantially improve quantum error-correcting codes without adding qubits or changing code distance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical optimization workflow for tailoring surface-code variants to the actual circuit noise and decoder used in a fault-tolerant quantum computer.
method: Treat circuit, noise model, and decoder as a black box.
Use Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI) to search the exponentially large Clifford-deformation space with few shots.
Benchmark on rotated surface codes under strongly Z-biased circuit-level noise with PyMatching.
infographic.evidence_signal: At distance 3, EBBI found the optimal deformation using up to about 1100× fewer shots than random search, and at distance 5 it converged to the authors’ believed-optimal codes while random search did not.
infographic.watch_item: The best deformation depends strongly on the specific noise model and decoder, so results may not transfer directly across hardware platforms or decoding pipelines.
infographic.paper_title: Decoder- and Noise-Aware Optimization Framework for Clifford-Deformed Quantum Error-Correcting Codes

title: Q-Capsule: A Localized Capsule-Based Quantum Neural Architecture for Barren Plateau Mitigation
authors: Awal Ahmed Fime, Tasfia Zaman Samiha, Saika Zaman, Dimitris Pados, George Sklivanitis, Abdur R. Shahid
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are often limited by barren plateaus: gradients vanish as circuit size and depth increase, making quantum neural networks difficult to train. We propose Q-Capsule, a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates this problem through register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, trainable data re-uploading, and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM)-guided adaptive depth growth. By restricting the dominant support of each observable to a small capsule and controlling inter-capsule entanglement, Q-Capsule preserves useful gradient signals while retaining communication between local quantum representations. As the register width increases, Q-Capsule consistently maintains stable gradient variance, whereas globally entangling baselines exhibit exponential suppression with a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit. Q-Capsule also produces more structured optimization landscapes, higher parameter efficiency, improved robustness to depolarizing noise, and lower measurement requirements. Its adaptive policy achieves 98.1% accuracy on binary classification and 97.7% on four-class classification, while using approximately 73% fewer two-qubit gates than the fixed-deep model on the multiclass task.

infographic.key_insight: Q-Capsule reduces barren-plateau risk by localizing each capsule’s observables and entanglement so gradients stay usable as circuit width grows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture offers a practical design pattern for trainable quantum neural networks that are more scalable, noise-tolerant, and measurement-efficient.
method: Partition the register into localized capsules with mostly local readout.
Use sparse inter-capsule coupling plus trainable data re-uploading to preserve communication.
Grow depth adaptively using QFIM-guided policy instead of fixing a deep global circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stable gradient variance with increasing width, a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit for global baselines, and adaptive-policy accuracy of 98.1% on binary and 97.7% on four-class classification.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful capsule partitioning and QFIM-based depth control, which could add tuning overhead and hardware/compiler complexity.
infographic.paper_title: Q-Capsule: A Localized Capsule-Based Quantum Neural Architecture for Barren Plateau Mitigation

title: QTN-RQNN: Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network
authors: Amit S. Patel, Himanshu R. Patel, Bikash K. Behera, Pranav Mehta, Ghanshyam Tejani, Deepak Parashar
abstract: Resource constraints and imperfect quantum operations remain major challenges for quantum machine learning (QML) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, particularly for fault-diagnosis tasks involving imbalanced and heterogeneous data. This work proposes QTN-RQNN, a Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network that integrates tensor-network-inspired nearest-neighbor interactions with recurrent quantum processing. The model sequentially encodes input features while propagating quantum memory across recurrent steps and incorporates QSMOTE for class balancing. QTN-RQNN is evaluated on four heterogeneous fault-diagnosis datasets SPID, CWRUBD, EFDD, and SFDD and compared with QNN, QTN-QNN, and RQNN baselines through classification, ablation, multi-seed, convergence, and quantum-resource analyses. Results show dataset-dependent predictive behavior, indicating that increased quantum architectural complexity does not universally improve classification. On SPID, QTN-RQNN improves the RQNN F1-score from 0.3077 to 0.4516 and ROC-AUC from 0.4485 to 0.6970, while the remaining datasets exhibit different performance-resource trade-offs and sensitivity to recurrent timesteps and circuit depth. Across all datasets, QTN-RQNN reduces the two-qubit-gate count from 32 to 24 per sample relative to RQNN, corresponding to a 25% reduction without increasing the four-qubit requirement; the same relative reduction is obtained for QTN-QNN over QNN. These findings establish QTN-RQNN as a resource-conscious recurrent quantum architecture and highlight the need to jointly consider predictive performance and circuit-resource requirements for near-term quantum fault diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: QTN-RQNN combines tensor-network-inspired quantum connectivity with recurrent memory to improve fault diagnosis on NISQ hardware while using fewer two-qubit gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper is relevant for building resource-aware quantum classifiers that balance predictive quality with circuit depth and gate-count constraints on noisy devices.
method: Sequentially encodes input features into a recurrent quantum circuit
Uses nearest-neighbor tensor-network interactions to shape quantum connectivity
Applies QSMOTE to rebalance imbalanced fault-diagnosis classes
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on four heterogeneous datasets (SPID, CWRUBD, EFDD, SFDD) against QNN, QTN-QNN, and RQNN baselines, with SPID showing F1 improving from 0.3077 to 0.4516 and ROC-AUC from 0.4485 to 0.6970.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is dataset-dependent, so added architectural complexity does not guarantee improvement and may require careful tuning of timesteps and circuit depth.
infographic.paper_title: QTN-RQNN: Quantum Tensor Network-Based Recurrent Quantum Neural Network

title: Entanglement entropy and magic of ZX-diagrams
authors: Marcin Szyniszewski, Razin A. Shaikh, Aleks Kissinger
abstract: Entanglement and non-stabilizerness are complementary resources underlying the complexity of quantum states, yet extracting either quantity from large quantum circuits generally requires exponentially scaling resources. In diagrammatic approaches to quantum computation, such as the ZX-calculus, both quantities likewise typically require expensive tensor contractions that are not native to graphical rewriting. Here we show that both entanglement and magic can be efficiently estimated directly from ZX-diagrams. Flow enables efficient extraction of a normal form separating a potentially extensively entangled graph-state backbone from non-Clifford Pauli gadgets. This structure yields additive upper and lower bounds on bipartite entanglement entropy, which we further tighten through a preprocessing procedure that removes or merges redundant non-Clifford contributions. The same normal form gives an upper bound on logarithmic stabilizer extent. We benchmark these methods in random unitary and monitored circuits, and a circuit combining Trotterized Hamiltonian evolution with Clifford layers, finding that the resulting bounds remain informative even at large qubit numbers, circuit depths, and internal spider counts. Our results provide scalable probes of entanglement and non-stabilizerness of ZX-diagrams and establish a bridge between ZX-calculus and quantum many-body resource characterization, with applications across quantum computing, quantum information, and condensed-matter physics.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that ZX-diagrams can directly yield efficient bounds on both entanglement entropy and magic by separating a graph-state backbone from non-Clifford Pauli gadgets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum algorithm designers and simulation tool builders a scalable way to estimate key resource costs without expensive full tensor contractions.
method: Use ZX-calculus flow to extract a normal form of the diagram.
Treat the normal form as a graph-state backbone plus non-Clifford Pauli gadgets.
Compute additive upper/lower entanglement bounds and an upper bound on logarithmic stabilizer extent, with preprocessing to merge or remove redundant gadgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors benchmark the method on random unitary circuits, monitored circuits, and Trotterized Hamiltonian evolution with Clifford layers, reporting informative bounds even at large qubit counts, depths, and spider counts.
infographic.watch_item: The bounds are informative rather than exact, so their usefulness depends on how well the ZX normal form captures the circuit structure and on the quality of preprocessing.
infographic.paper_title: Entanglement entropy and magic of ZX-diagrams

title: Measure Now, Mitigate Later: Virtual Error Cancellation for Logical Quantum Circuits
authors: Oles Shtanko, Saswata Roy, Shashwat Kumar, Zlatko Minev
abstract: Early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms are a key step in scalable quantum computing, but are ultimately constrained by residual, uncorrectable logical errors. Logical quantum error mitigation can eliminate this bias, however its standard requirements include prior noise characterization, more complex experiments, and substantial sampling overhead. Although no mitigation technique can simultaneously overcome all three constraints, we demonstrate that the first two---noise learning and need for modified circuits---can be completely bypassed for logical circuits by leveraging only syndrome records. Specifically, we introduce virtual error cancellation: a method that, unlike previous bias-free approaches, operates entirely in classical post-processing on universal quantum circuits. We develop and numerically test end-to-end protocols that reduce the sampling overhead beyond fundamental limitations of existing syndrome-aware mitigation techniques, including syndrome-based postselection. In particular, we propose a scheme that pairs the low-latency decoder used in the experiment with a high-complexity decoder run in post-processing. In numerical simulations of a distance-7 rotated surface code, we show that our full-stack dual-decoder algorithm exhibits an error that diminishes as the number of samples increases, capable of reaching more than three orders of magnitude of suppression compared to the decoded logical error rate in an experimentally achievable setting. These results establish syndrome records as a resource for correcting universal computational estimates after quantum execution.

infographic.key_insight: Syndrome records alone can be used in post-processing to cancel logical errors in quantum circuits without learning the noise model or modifying the executed circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables bias-free logical error mitigation for early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms with lower experimental complexity and reduced reliance on prior calibration.
method: Use only measured syndrome records as the input for classical post-processing.
Pair a fast experimental decoder with a more accurate high-complexity decoder offline.
Apply virtual error cancellation to estimate unbiased logical observables after execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulations of a distance-7 rotated surface code, the dual-decoder protocol showed error decreasing with sample count and achieved more than three orders of magnitude suppression versus the decoded logical error rate in an experimentally achievable regime.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on decoder quality and may incur substantial classical post-processing and sampling overhead in practical deployments.
infographic.paper_title: Measure Now, Mitigate Later: Virtual Error Cancellation for Logical Quantum Circuits

title: Parameter-Dependent Noise Resilience in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: Jorja Kirk, Ashley Montanaro
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum algorithm used for solving combinatorial optimization problems, which is thought to be a promising application of near-term quantum hardware. However, high rates of noise in these devices can obscure meaningful results. Therefore, it is crucial to understand and suppress the effects of noise on the algorithm's output. Here, we find that the stability of the algorithm in the presence of noise is dependent on its variational parameters. Using a Pauli noise model, we derive an upper bound on the total variation distance between the noisy and noiseless circuit output as a function of these parameters. Results from noisy simulations support this bound and give insight into the best methods to use for parameter generation in the presence of noise. We also introduce new methods of optimization using error penalties and truncated search based on this bound to manufacture error resilience. We extend this analysis to the quantum adiabatic algorithm (QAA) by taking the continuous limit of the QAOA.

infographic.key_insight: QAOA’s sensitivity to noise depends strongly on its variational parameters, and this dependence can be bounded analytically to guide more noise-resilient circuit choices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result helps practitioners select and optimize QAOA parameters and search strategies that are more robust on noisy near-term quantum hardware.
method: Derive an upper bound on total variation distance between noisy and noiseless QAOA outputs under a Pauli noise model.
Use noisy simulations to validate the parameter-dependent bound and compare parameter-generation strategies.
Introduce optimization approaches with error penalties and truncated search, and extend the analysis to the quantum adiabatic algorithm via the continuous limit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that noisy simulation results support the analytic bound and provide guidance for choosing parameter-generation methods under noise.
infographic.watch_item: The bound and resilience strategies are derived for a specific Pauli noise model, so their effectiveness may vary under more realistic or hardware-specific noise processes.
infographic.paper_title: Parameter-Dependent Noise Resilience in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion
authors: Jingyan Xu, Yuanhong Wu, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Sean Patten, Christina Schweikert, D. Frank Hsu
abstract: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are highly sensitive to circuit architecture, yet most quantum machine learning pipelines select a single best design and discard the remaining candidates. This paper addresses whether the structural diversity across quantum circuit search spaces can be used to produce stronger predictions through model fusion. We apply Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (CFA), a model fusion framework that selects and combines multiple scoring systems using rank-score function (RSF) and cognitive diversity (CD), to a pool of 29 architecturally diverse classical models and quantum circuits. Using a diversity-aware model selection method, we identify subsets of maximally diverse models and combine them with both score and rank combination. Experiments on four binary classification benchmarks covering different domains demonstrate that CFA-based hybrid classical-quantum fusion consistently outperform the best individual model on every dataset considered with improvements up to 6.03% in accuracy. When comparing with relevant literatures, the CFA framework further achieves superior performance across all four datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Selecting and fusing diverse quantum and classical models can outperform choosing a single best variational quantum circuit, with diversity helping drive better predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum ML pipeline design, the result suggests architecture search should preserve and exploit model diversity rather than only optimizing one top-performing circuit.
method: Built a pool of 29 structurally diverse classical models and quantum circuits.
Used Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (CFA) with rank-score function (RSF) and cognitive diversity (CD) to select maximally diverse subsets.
Combined selected models using score and rank fusion to form hybrid classical-quantum ensembles.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four binary classification benchmarks, the CFA-based fusion consistently beat the best individual model, with accuracy gains up to 6.03% and superior results versus related literature on all datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on identifying a diverse candidate pool, so gains may be limited if quantum circuit search spaces or evaluation budgets are small.
infographic.paper_title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion

title: Circuit Design Problems in Binary Polynomial Quantum Optimization
authors: Dylan Laplace Mermoud, Dimitri Watel, Sourour Elloumi, Andrea Simonetto
abstract: Solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum computers mainly relies on their quadratic unconstrained binary formulation. Lately, binary polynomial formulations start to take the center stage, having a better scaling with respect to the number of used qubits. However, while quadratic forms are straightforward to implement on quantum circuits, polynomial forms of degree $d$ incur in circuit depth overheads, due to the lack of $d$-qubit gates, for $d\geq 3$, on current hardware. In this paper, we study the problem of designing the shallowest quantum circuit for a given polynomial form. We formulate it as a classical binary linear problem and we prove the \textsf{NP}-completeness of a variant of it. On the algorithmic side, we offer a scalable and performant heuristic method to tackle it, Tempura, as well as faster binary linear problem formulations, which offer computational feasibility while sacrificing optimality. Our performance evaluation shows that the algorithms yield far shorter circuits than the state-of-the-art approaches, and Tempura is mostly comparable with them in terms of runtime.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns the problem of compiling binary polynomial quantum optimization into a classical binary linear design problem to minimize circuit depth for near-term hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides practical tools for building shallower quantum circuits from higher-degree objective functions, which can reduce overhead on current devices that lack native multi-qubit gates.
method: Formulate shallow-circuit design as a binary linear optimization problem.
Prove NP-completeness for a variant of the circuit-design problem.
Introduce Tempura, a scalable heuristic, plus faster approximate formulations for feasible computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the proposed algorithms produce much shorter circuits than state-of-the-art methods while Tempura remains mostly comparable in runtime.
infographic.watch_item: The faster formulations trade optimality for scalability, so implementation quality depends on the acceptable depth-vs-computation compromise.
infographic.paper_title: Circuit Design Problems in Binary Polynomial Quantum Optimization

title: Scaling Quantum Optimization to the Thousand-Qubit Scale with Distributed Quantum Sampling
authors: Amana Liaqat, Ahmed Darwish, Stephen DiAdamo, Dan Holme, Kieran McDowall, Emre Sahin
abstract: The Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition (MBD) seeks a sparse weighted sum of matchings and is a challenging optimization problem with applications in network scheduling and energy trading. We scale a quantum-assisted decomposition method by combining single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) optimization, spectral graph partitioning, and greedy feasibility repair. We demonstrate the pipeline on the 1,354-node PEGASE bus test case (representing a 1,354-bus transmission grid with 1,710 transmission lines), whose 1,710 edges define a native 1,710-variable matching optimization problem requiring 1,710 qubits in the unpartitioned encoding. Partitioning enables distributed execution on IBM superconducting quantum processors. The best reported hardware result uses a 50-qubit partition bound, while reducing partitions to 20 qubits degrades convergence in the partition-size comparison. Larger partitions are more demanding for matrix product state (MPS) simulation, and bond-dimension tests show that truncating quantum correlations reduces candidate quality. The results therefore motivate retaining a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition as the overall problem scales. On the PEGASE-1354 benchmark, repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than both simulated annealing and uniform random sampling baselines, while spatial circuit packing reduces hardware execution time by approximately a factor of three. These results demonstrate that combining spectral partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems on current hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A distributed QAOA-plus-classical-repair pipeline can scale constrained quantum optimization to a 1,710-variable matching problem by partitioning it into hardware-executable subproblems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical route for applying near-term quantum processors to large network optimization tasks such as grid scheduling and energy trading.
method: Spectral graph partition the large matching problem into smaller qubit-sized blocks.
Run single-layer QAOA sampling within each partition on hardware or simulation.
Use E-FCFW plus greedy feasibility repair to assemble valid global decompositions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PEGASE-1354, repaired QAOA samples outperformed simulated annealing and uniform random sampling, and spatial circuit packing cut hardware execution time by about 3×.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on partition size and retained quantum correlations, so overly small partitions or aggressive MPS truncation can degrade solution quality.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Quantum Optimization to the Thousand-Qubit Scale with Distributed Quantum Sampling

title: Error Mitigation by Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) in Indirect-Control System
authors: Arijit Das, Masaki Owari
abstract: The indirect-control paradigm offers a scalable approach to quantum computation by restricting external operations to a small subset of qubits, whereas the entire system evolves under its intrinsic many-body Hamiltonian. This framework reduces hardware complexity and limits the noise introduced through control channels. Recently, Anan et al. proposed an implementation of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) within this indirect-control architecture. However, the impact and integration of quantum error mitigation techniques in such a setting remain largely unexplored. In particular, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), a widely used error mitigation strategy, has not yet been systematically adapted to indirect-control VQE. A key requirement of ZNE is the controlled amplification of noise, which is commonly achieved through circuit-level techniques such as unitary folding. In the indirect-control framework, however, quantum operations are largely governed by continuous time-evolution under the system Hamiltonian, making the construction of physically realizable inverse operations non-trivial. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of implementing ZNE within the indirect-controlVQEframework.We address the challenges associated with unitary folding in the presence of time-evolution operators and, with a minimal relaxation of the indirect-control constraint, we propose a ZNE-based error-mitigation strategy that exploits the symmetry of the one-dimensional XY spin chain.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that zero-noise extrapolation can be adapted to indirect-control VQE by leveraging symmetry in a 1D XY spin chain, despite the difficulty of defining inverse operations for time-evolution-based circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This extends error mitigation to a more hardware-efficient quantum control model, helping reduce control-channel complexity while preserving practical access to near-term quantum simulation.
method: Analyze how ZNE can work when gates are replaced by continuous Hamiltonian evolution
Address the unitary-folding challenge under indirect-control constraints
Use a minimal relaxation of the control restriction plus XY-chain symmetry to construct a physically realizable mitigation strategy
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract indicates a feasibility study focused on adapting ZNE to indirect-control VQE and on resolving the implementation barriers posed by time-evolution operators.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a minimal relaxation of the indirect-control constraint and may be specific to the symmetry structure of the one-dimensional XY model.
infographic.paper_title: Error Mitigation by Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) in Indirect-Control System

title: An Efficient Quantum Circuit for Flow Model Execution Using Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Rui Che, Ludvig af Klinteberg
abstract: Flow models generate trajectories from an initial distribution to a target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation defined by a velocity field. Flow matching learns this velocity field by modeling the transport dynamics between the two distributions. Wavefunction flow establishes a formal connection between flow models and quantum dynamics by introducing a continuity Hamiltonian, which drives the Schrödinger evolution of quantum states. In this paper, we investigate accurate and efficient quantum simulation of the wavefunction flow, thereby realizing the efficient implementation of flow models on quantum computers. We first leverage a quantum read-only memory (QROM)-based phase kickback framework for the wavefunction flow simulation, generating probability densities that closely match those produced by the corresponding conventional flow model. To address the high circuit-resource cost, we further incorporate a trained quantum neural network (QNN) into the phase kickback framework, replacing QROM for data encoding. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed method implements flow models on quantum computers more efficiently, since it maintains the accuracy of wavefunction flow simulation compared with the QROM-based framework, and significantly reduces the circuit resources.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that flow models can be efficiently executed on quantum hardware by simulating wavefunction flow with a quantum circuit, and that a trained QNN can replace expensive QROM data encoding without losing accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a more resource-efficient pathway for deploying generative flow models on quantum computers, which is important for scalable quantum simulation and quantum machine learning workflows.
method: Build a quantum simulation of wavefunction flow using a QROM-based phase kickback framework.
Replace QROM with a trained quantum neural network (QNN) for data encoding to reduce circuit cost.
Compare the resulting probability densities against the conventional flow model to verify fidelity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments in the abstract indicate that the QNN-based approach matches the accuracy of the QROM-based wavefunction flow simulation while using significantly fewer circuit resources.
infographic.watch_item: The main implementation concern is training and deploying the QNN reliably on hardware, since resource savings must not introduce approximation error or stability issues in the quantum circuit.
infographic.paper_title: An Efficient Quantum Circuit for Flow Model Execution Using Quantum Neural Networks

title: Measurement-Efficient Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search for Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Lukas Theißinger, Thore Gerlach, Christian Bauckhage
abstract: Differentiable quantum architecture search (DQAS) is a promising framework for the automated design of quantum circuits, particularly for variational quantum optimization algorithms. However, its practical deployment on quantum hardware is limited by the large number of circuit measurements required during optimization, making hardware execution costly. In this work, we show that for a broad class of combinatorial optimization problems and commonly used rotational gate parameterizations, the measurement cost of DQAS can be significantly reduced without changing the optimization objective. We derive the proposed measurement reduction scheme theoretically and validate it experimentally on 3-SAT and MaxCut benchmark problems. Our approach reduces the requested gradient measurement cost by about 39 to 41% while introducing only negligible classical post-processing overhead, lowering the practical cost of executing DQAS on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that differentiable quantum architecture search can be made much more measurement-efficient for combinatorial optimization circuits without changing the underlying optimization objective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This lowers the quantum hardware cost of training variational optimization circuits, making DQAS more practical for near-term quantum systems.
method: Derive a measurement-reduction scheme for broad combinatorial optimization settings.
Exploit common rotational gate parameterizations to reuse or avoid gradient measurements.
Keep the optimization objective unchanged while adding only minimal classical post-processing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on 3-SAT and MaxCut show about 39–41% lower gradient measurement cost with negligible classical overhead.
infographic.watch_item: The savings are demonstrated for a broad but still specific class of problems and gate parameterizations, so applicability may be limited outside that setting.
infographic.paper_title: Measurement-Efficient Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search for Combinatorial Optimization

title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing
authors: Emanuele G. Dalla Torre, Bat-El Friedman, Daniel Porat
abstract: Qubits are powerful computational resources because each additional qubit doubles the size of the accessible state space. This expressive power comes at a cost: adding qubits also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and exposure to hardware noise. These limitations are especially critical for near-term quantum computers, making the number of qubits required to formulate a problem a central practical concern. In this work, we present a method for efficiently mapping logistics and routing problems onto qubits through structure-aware encoding reduction. We demonstrate the method on a benchmark problem of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures. For this benchmark, the reduced formulation substantially lowers both the qubit count and the compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. By running the reduced model on the same trapped-ion quantum computer as the benchmark, we obtain a 100X improvement in the success probability. This finding shows how careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization.

infographic.key_insight: A structure-aware encoding reduction can dramatically cut qubit usage for routing optimization without changing the underlying problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For near-term quantum hardware, lowering qubit count and circuit complexity can make logistics and routing workloads more feasible and improve solution reliability.
method: Reformulate the routing problem with fewer qubits using problem structure.
Preserve the original optimization objective while reducing encoding overhead.
Compile and run the reduced model on trapped-ion hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the same trapped-ion quantum computer, the reduced formulation achieved a 100× improvement in success probability while also lowering qubit count and circuit complexity.
infographic.watch_item: The approach appears problem-structure dependent, so gains may not transfer directly to routing or optimization tasks without similar exploitable structure.
infographic.paper_title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing

title: Quantum Co-Design of Inhomogeneous Many-Body Neutrino Fast Flavor Transformation
authors: Zoha Laraib, Sherwood Richers, Alessandro Baroni, Kathleen Hamilton, In-Saeng Suh
abstract: Dense-neutrino flavor evolution is a quantum many-body problem whose fully correlated treatment becomes rapidly more expensive with increasing particle number and spatial structure. We develop a \texttt{QCNO} quantum simulation code that maps a inhomogeneous forward-scattering neutrino Hamiltonian with advection and finite-range interactions to TEBD2 product-formula quantum circuits, and connects ideal many-body simulation, backend-aware execution, and fault-tolerant resource estimation within the same physical model. We reproduce the exact many-body evolution of the suppressed mean-field-like transverse fast flavor instability through $N=30$ and show that even a single open-boundary interaction generates Rënyi entanglement and non-stabilizer magic, although noisy backends still produce polarization RMSEs of order $0.1$--$0.3$. The restricted active interaction graph of this problem allows us to estimate the circuit depth and $T$ gate cost through $N=50$ for both NISQ and fault-tolerant approaches. The measured TEBD2 error in our fiducial ideal simulation of order $10^{-3}$ motivates a synthesis tolerance $\varepsilon_{\rm syn}\sim10^{-7}$, corresponding to about $70$ $T$ gates per $R_Z$ rotation. The generated circuit contains $1.4\times10^4$ $T$ gates per qubit for open boundaries (twice that for closed boundaries), requiring an application-level logical-$T$ error target of order $10^{-7}$ for early fault-tolerant architectures.

infographic.key_insight: QCNO maps inhomogeneous neutrino fast flavor transformation onto TEBD2 quantum circuits, enabling a single framework for exact dynamics, backend execution, and fault-tolerant resource estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work gives a concrete path to assess whether quantum hardware can eventually simulate strongly correlated neutrino flavor evolution, while quantifying the circuit depth and error budgets needed for near- and long-term devices.
method: Map the forward-scattering neutrino Hamiltonian with advection and finite-range interactions to TEBD2 product-formula circuits.
Benchmark ideal evolution against exact many-body dynamics for the transverse fast flavor instability.
Estimate NISQ performance and fault-tolerant T-gate costs up to N=50 using the restricted interaction graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reproduction of exact many-body evolution through N=30, noisy-backend polarization RMSEs around 0.1-0.3, TEBD2 error near 10^-3, and about 1.4×10^4 T gates per qubit for open boundaries.
infographic.watch_item: The resource estimates depend on the specific interaction graph and synthesis tolerance, so hardware noise and fault-tolerant overheads may shift the feasibility window significantly.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Co-Design of Inhomogeneous Many-Body Neutrino Fast Flavor Transformation
